content: Parents generally trusted the skills of nurses and appreciated their precision and educational approach during procedures. However, they did not always fully understand the diagnostic purpose of nasopharyngeal aspirate (NPA) sample collection for tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis. Some parents mistakenly believed that the NPA procedure was intended to improve their child’s breathing. Nurses themselves viewed NPA as an unpleasant or painful procedure for children, often requiring repeated aspirations. Most nurses reported needing additional support from a colleague or parent to restrain the child during the procedure. Despite these challenges, nurses had a positive perception of NPA, recognizing its contribution to improving child health and potentially reducing mortality. Many nurses believed that NPA, being less invasive and quicker to perform, could replace other sample collection methods like gastric aspirates. In conclusion, NPA samples were successfully collected in 95% of children, with 4% (39 out of 269) of children diagnosed with TB. Combining NPA and stool samples was found to be safe and highly feasible in children with severe pneumonia, contributing to microbiological confirmation in 30% (24 out of 82) of TB-diagnosed children. While NPA was perceived as unpleasant or painful, the overall acceptability of the procedure was positive. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends collecting appropriate specimens from suspected sites of TB involvement for rapid diagnostic testing using molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) or culture, and histopathological examination for children with extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) whenever possible. For pulmonary TB (PTB) in children, the Xpert MTB/RIF test is recommended as the initial diagnostic test for TB and rifampicin resistance detection in sputum, gastric aspirate, nasopharyngeal aspirate, and stool, rather than smear microscopy or culture. The Xpert Ultra assay, an enhanced version of Xpert MTB/RIF, improves sensitivity and reliability for detecting TB and rifampicin resistance, especially in pediatric specimens where TB disease is often paucibacillary. Trace results from Xpert Ultra are considered bacteriological confirmation of TB in children and people living with HIV. The TrueNat MTB and MTB Plus assays, which use chip-based real-time micro-PCR, are also recommended as initial diagnostic tests for TB in sputum specimens. These assays are designed for use in peripheral laboratories with minimal infrastructure and training requirements. For people living with HIV, the urine lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assay may be used as a point-of-care test to assist in TB diagnosis, particularly in urgent cases where rapid diagnosis is critical for survival. However, LF-LAM is not recommended for use in children or adults without TB symptoms or with higher CD4 cell counts. Chest X-rays (CXR) remain an important diagnostic tool for TB in children, especially when bacteriological tests are negative or unavailable. Radiographic changes suggestive of TB include enlarged lymph nodes, dense alveolar opacification, miliary patterns, cavitation, and pleural or pericardial effusion. Adolescents with TB often present with radiographic changes similar to adults, such as apical infiltrates or large pleural effusions. High-quality CXRs, ideally interpreted by trained pediatric radiologists, are essential for thorough clinical evaluation and determining disease severity. Early detection of HIV is critical for managing TB/HIV coinfection, as all children with HIV-associated TB are eligible for antiretroviral therapy (ART) and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. Integrated treatment decision algorithms have been developed to diagnose pulmonary TB in children under 10 years of age, particularly in high TB burden settings with limited resources. These algorithms aim to reduce the gap in case detection and improve treatment access. They are not suitable for diagnosing extrapulmonary TB or managing asymptomatic children identified through active case-finding strategies. The algorithms emphasize the importance of bacteriological confirmation using WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests whenever possible.
